title: Driving characteristics and their trade-offs
blurb: Every architecture buys one quality by spending another; this one names both. Learnability and safety are in direct tension here — asking for a token is friction, and friction is what stops a careless action — so the diagram records the trade rather than pretending it was free.

title: An auth decision, written as an ADR
blurb: A shared session cookie was rejected in favour of a scoped token, and the reason was coupling, not security theatre. The cookie would have bound the extension to the app's session model; a bearer token couples them only by the name of one header. The negative consequences are recorded alongside the positive ones.

title: STRIDE over a data-flow diagram
blurb: Four trust zones, and the most important one is the zone I do not control. Each STRIDE class is mapped to the specific control that answers it — spoofing to a scoped bearer token rather than an ambient cookie, information disclosure to keeping licensed text transient and never persisting it.

title: The domain as a state machine
blurb: The rules live in one place instead of being scattered across request handlers. Modelling the core as explicit states and transitions means an invalid transition is unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely.

title: How a change reaches production
blurb: A commit to a manifest becomes a running pod, and a change made by hand gets reverted. That reversion is the feature: if the cluster can drift from git without anyone noticing, git is documentation rather than a source of truth.

title: Platform topology
blurb: Thirty-eight applications on one node, reconciled from git, with no secrets in the repository. Vault issues credentials that external-secrets materialises into the cluster; every service sits behind one identity provider; and the deliberately vulnerable workloads used for security practice are isolated by namespace under default-deny network policy. Network addresses are redacted here.

title: Fluency — container view
blurb: The learning app at C4 container level: what runs, what holds state, and which boundaries carry authentication. Useful mainly as the map the other Fluency diagrams zoom into.

title: One review queue, two sources
blurb: A learner should never have to know which queue they are in. Two independent card sources feed a single scheduling spine, which is harder than running two queues and is the entire reason the product feels like one thing.

title: Deck generation, with a control stage
blurb: Generation without a control stage produces plausible cards that teach the wrong thing. The second stage exists purely to constrain the first — the expensive part was deciding what it should refuse, not what it should produce.

title: Reading companion — bookend retrieval
blurb: Turns what you just read into scheduled recall without ever storing the licensed text. The passage is transient input; only the questions derived from it persist. That constraint shaped the whole design, and it is the boundary the threat model is built around.

title: Math rendering — the delimiter contract
blurb: The check meant to guard this is manual, tests the wrong renderer, and misses a real bug — and the diagram says so. Documenting a weak fitness function is more useful than claiming a strong one, because the next person to touch it needs to know what it does not cover.

title: Narration bake — serial versus pipelined
blurb: The same work drawn twice, so the latency difference is visible rather than asserted. Pipelining helps here because the stages are independent; the diagram exists to show that, not to claim it.

title: User flow — onboard once, then read
blurb: One setup step, then a loop the user repeats without ceremony. Everything that could have been a settings screen was pushed into that single step deliberately.

title: One round-trip, frontstage and backstage
blurb: Service-blueprint style: what the user sees above the line, what the system does below it. The gap between the two is where the perceived latency budget gets spent.

title: Integration layer — context view
blurb: One adapter layer so several self-hosted applications can be driven through a single interface. Designed against a written spec; nothing is deployed.

title: The abstraction that survives three APIs
blurb: Three services authenticate three different ways, and the useful work was deciding what not to abstract. A static bearer token, an exchanged JWT and an API key share exactly one thing — an HTTP request carrying a credential — so that is all the interface promises.

title: Tool surface and least privilege
blurb: Credentials stay server-side and never enter model context. Every capability is scoped so one compromised path cannot spend another service's credentials — the design assumes the caller is non-deterministic and may be wrong.

title: knowledge-drift — container view
blurb: A system for noticing when documented knowledge and reality have diverged. Container view, designed against a written spec.

title: knowledge-drift — the governance loop
blurb: Detecting drift is easy; deciding who gets to act on it is the hard part. This is the authority model — who declares something stale, and what the loop is permitted to change on its own.

title: Rift Bingo
blurb: A smaller project, drawn as it actually is rather than as it was meant to be. Included because a corrected architecture is more honest than an idealised one.

title: Two sites, one git, no shared quorum
blurb: A second node in another cloud, where the decision that mattered was what not to build. One cluster stretched across both sites is the obvious move and it is arithmetically wrong: two etcd members require both to be up, which is strictly worse than one, and a partition would then break both sites at once. Independent clusters, a single git source, and asynchronous replication that needs no quorum at all.
